stories.title: Trump Calls the Board: Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia
stories.story:
On the morning of November 12, Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia under a cloud: an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials described as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset had become public, and his board moved swiftly, saying his behavior was "inconsistent with the company's code of conduct." Four days later, the newly installed chairman told investors the board had "no intention" of reinstating him. The matter seemed closed.

It wasn't. Over the following week, President Trump — who holds personal Nvidia stock and has accepted $25 million in donations from Huang — orchestrated what CNN described as an "unprecedented West Wing pressure campaign." He dialed into Nvidia's Sunday board meeting personally, consulted his Attorney General and Director of National Intelligence to produce a finding that Huang posed "no national security risk," and publicly declared on Truth Social that rehiring Huang would be "the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A." By Sunday night the board had flipped. By Monday morning the announcement was public. Trump told CNBC: "I made the deal."

Markets told their own story. Nvidia surged 31.5% in a single session — its largest one-day gain in 23 years — restoring nearly $1 trillion in market capitalization. The Nasdaq jumped 6.5%. Taiwan's stock exchange climbed 9%.

The deeper implication is structural: a sitting president has now demonstrated that the governance of the world's most critical semiconductor company is, in a crisis, a political variable. The board that said no became the board that said yes within 96 hours. Congressional Democrats have promised investigations; some Republican senators have expressed open skepticism. Huang is set to testify before Congress next week. The national security questions — an unfinished counterintelligence probe, a chip-sales arrangement with China — remain unresolved. The stock is up. The story is not over.
stories.hook: When one phone call from the Oval Office can reverse a corporate board's unanimous decision, 'independent governance' is a theory, not a fact.

stories.title: CrowdStrike Swallows Zscaler in Cybersecurity's Biggest-Ever Merger
stories.story:
For two decades, corporate cybersecurity was sold in layers: one vendor to guard the endpoint, another to police the network perimeter, a third to manage identity. Customers stitched them together with integrations and prayer. That architecture is now being dismantled at scale.

On November 23, CrowdStrike announced it would acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction valued at $43.9 billion — the largest cybersecurity deal ever recorded. The logic is structural, not merely financial. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform owns the endpoint and workload layer; Zscaler's Zero Trust Security Service Edge controls what flows across the network. Together, they would begin life with more than $10 billion in combined annual recurring revenue, surpassing Palo Alto Networks' projected next-generation security ARR and seizing the industry's top spot by that measure.

The timing is not coincidental. AI has industrialized cyberattacks: phishing campaigns now write themselves, malware adapts in real time to evade signature detection, and the attack surface has sprawled as enterprises push workloads into the cloud. Selling point solutions into this environment is increasingly untenable for customers who need fewer consoles, not more. The two firms already share more than 2,000 customers across 16 integrations — the merger converts a partnership into a single throat to choke.

The deal carries a 34% premium to Zscaler's pre-announcement price, and CrowdStrike estimates it will expand its total addressable market by more than $185 billion by 2029. Antitrust review under Hart-Scott-Rodino is required; the transaction is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028. What it implies for every mid-tier cybersecurity vendor is starker: consolidation at the top tends to hollow out the middle.
stories.hook: When the two biggest locks in the industry merge, every smaller locksmith has to wonder who's next.

stories.title: The Bond Market Refuses to Believe the Fed Is Done
stories.story:
Monday's equity explosion — the Nasdaq's best single day since April 2025 — had a shadow running beneath it: the bond market told a sharply different story. Even as stocks surged on the Nvidia news, the 2-year Treasury yield jumped more than 7 basis points, and the 10-year held near 4.93%, anchored well above the 5% threshold it has been orbiting for weeks. The message from fixed income was blunt: relief rallies in equities do not change the inflation calculus.

The backdrop is a Fed that re-entered tightening mode in September after a three-year pause, raising rates by 25 basis points to a 3.75%–4% target range. Then October's inflation print came in hotter than expected, with core CPI rising 0.3% month-on-month. Fed Governor Chris Waller put a 50-basis-point December hike openly on the table. The October FOMC minutes, released last week, showed "a couple of participants" willing to go bigger if the data warranted. Futures markets now price roughly a 90% chance of a hike on December 9, with more than 80 basis points of further tightening priced through September 2027.

The transmission mechanism is already biting. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed to 7.28% — not because the Fed has acted again, but because bond traders pushed the 10-year yield above 5% in anticipation. Mortgage lenders price off the 10-year, not the overnight rate, so the future hike is already in monthly payments today. JPMorgan's asset management arm flags real yields near 2.89% as the structural anchor keeping gold capped and credit spreads stressed. Morgan Stanley sees the 10-year ending 2027 at 5% — meaning this is not an overshoot to be faded but a new regime to be lived in.

What today's short squeeze in equities obscures is that the AI capex boom driving stock enthusiasm is itself a source of bond supply pressure: companies financing data centers are issuing debt at scale, adding to Treasury competition at exactly the moment the government's own deficit spending is highest. The Fed is tightening into a supply wall.
stories.hook: The stock market had a party on Monday, but the bond market didn't get the invitation — and the bond market is the one setting your mortgage rate.
stories.source: Bloomberg, CNBC, Nuveen Fixed Income Weekly
